========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Hi, Doctor. Thanks for fitting me in. So, I’m a medical services manager—I oversee a few different outpatient clinics, handle the administrative side of things, make sure the providers have what they need. I've been doing it a while, worked my way up after getting my associate's, and I actually really like the fast-paced, putting-out-fires parts of the job. 

But the main reason I finally decided I needed to come in and talk to somebody is that... well, whenever I have to do anything that takes real, heavy, sitting-down brain work, it just feels like I hit a massive brick wall. I mean, things like pulling together the monthly compliance reports, or right now I'm supposed to be planning this big multi-site community health event, which involves coordinating schedules across three different facilities, managing the logistics, figuring out the budget. It's really important stuff. I *know* how much it matters. If those reports aren't in, our funding gets flagged. 

But I sit at my desk, I open the file, and my brain just completely rejects it. I'll find literally anything else to do—I'll go check on the front desk staff, I'll reorganize the supply room, I'll answer emails from three weeks ago that don't even matter anymore. I just keep putting the deep thinking work off and off and off, pushing it to the next day, and then the next day. Even though I know the deadline is looming and my team is counting on me, I just avoid it. It’s like I physically cannot force myself to engage with that kind of heavy mental lifting until it becomes a total crisis, and honestly, the stress of constantly avoiding my most important tasks is just getting completely exhausting.

I mean... if I'm being completely honest with myself, and I really have thought about this because, you know, people always assume that when someone close to you passes away you just walk around with this dark cloud over your head forever... but honestly? No. I really don't feel that way.

Like, when I'm at the alley and someone tells a joke, or when I'm at Luigi's with my wife having that veal I mentioned, I'm genuinely just happy in that moment. I'm not secretly crying inside or feeling hollow or anything like that. I'm fully present and enjoying myself. I've made my peace with his passing, I really have. We even named the spring bowling tournament after him—the Mark Peterson Memorial Classic—which was a huge hit last year, we actually raised a lot of money for the youth league, which he would have absolutely loved. 

So the only time I feel anything even remotely close to a "heaviness" is literally just when I'm staring at his old binders, or staring at the clinic compliance reports on my monitor. And that's not sadness about Mark, and it's not some underlying depression. It's just sheer, unadulterated frustration that my brain won't let me do the work. It's annoyance at myself. So, no, there isn't this lingering sadness following me around. I miss the guy, obviously, but my mood is fine. It's just the logistics, the actual sitting down and doing the heavy administrative work he left behind, along with my actual day job, that's what's tripping me up. Not grief. Just... whatever this invisible wall is.

Honestly, doctor, it's exactly the same across the board. That's actually... well, to be perfectly frank, that's the main reason I’m here talking to you today. My brain just halts. I'll stare at the cursor blinking on the screen, and even though I know I need to do it, I just keep putting it off and putting it off. I’ll go reorganize the supply closet, or I'll go walk down the hall to chat with the front desk staff about the new intake forms, or I'll check my emails for the fiftieth time—literally anything to avoid that heavy analytical work. 

So, no, I wouldn't say the procrastination is worse with Mark's stuff at all. It's just that Mark's stuff happens to require that same deep, sustained focus, and right now, my brain just absolutely refuses to do it, no matter where the work is coming from or who it's for. If it involves sitting still and thinking hard, I hit that wall, every single time.

She thought maybe the grief was just, I don't know, scrambling my brain. And while losing Mark was... well, like I said, it was the hardest thing I've ever been through, this whole focus thing? No, it's definitely not new. Not at all. \n\nIf I really go back, like way back to elementary school... it was actually kind of a running theme. I remember these parent-teacher conferences so vividly. It didn't matter if it was third grade, fourth grade, fifth grade—it was the exact same speech every single year. The teachers would sit across those tiny little desks from my mom and dad and say, 'You know, he’s such a bright boy, he really is, he catches on so fast... but he’s just always daydreaming.' And they were right! I’d be staring out the window at the playground, or looking at a spot on the wall, completely in my own world while they were teaching. \n\nAnd the schoolwork... oh man, my backpack looked like a paper shredder had exploded inside it. I was constantly losing worksheets. The crazy part was, I would actually do the homework! I'd sit at the kitchen table, get it all done, and then the next day I'd just... forget to turn it in. It would just sit there crumpled at the bottom of my bag under a gym shoe or something. It got so bad that my mother—bless her heart, she had the patience of a saint—she had to institute this incredibly strict routine. Every single night, without fail, she would make me dump my backpack out on the kitchen island, and she would physically check every single folder and pocket. She had to verify that the homework was done and put in the right place, because if she didn't check my backpack every single night, I was absolutely going to forget to hand it in. \n\nSo, yeah, I guess long story short, it definitely didn't start with Mark's passing. It's been this way pretty much my whole life, just this... this constant, exhausting battle to keep my head out of the clouds and my papers in one place, you know? It's just that now, instead of third-grade math worksheets, it's clinic compliance reports, and my mom isn't around to check my briefcase.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned this has been going on since elementary school—but I want to ask: back in high school and college, when you were working toward your associate's degree, was this difficulty with focus and keeping track of your work about the same level as it was in elementary school, or did it get noticeably worse around the time Mark passed away two years ago?\n\nPatient: Well, that's... that is a really good distinction to make, actually. Because, sure, like I was just saying, I was always that daydreaming kid, and honestly, high school and getting my associate's degree? Definitely a struggle. I was the king of last-minute cramming and losing my course syllabus on the very first day. But I always managed to scrape by, you know? I sort of figured out my own messy ways to cope and keep my head just above water. \n\nBut this... the way it is right now? Where I'm just completely hitting a brick wall at work and my brain is just constantly flipping channels? That's been the last year and 11 months, right after he died and I took all that extra stuff on.\n\nDoctor: Before Mark passed away—so more than two years ago—when you were working at the clinics doing those same compliance reports and administrative tasks, were you able to sit down and complete that work without nearly as much struggle, or were you already hitting that same brick wall back then?\n\nPatient: Gosh, you know...
